extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and parties before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) in AIA trial proceedings (IPR, PGR, CBM, derivation)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for litigating AIA trial proceedings before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (inter partes review, post-grant review, covered business-method review, and derivation proceedings), including procedures on communications, discovery, protective orders, claim construction, institution decisions, motions, and evidentiary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on Ex Parte Communications
rubrics_metrics.description: All substantive communications with the Board regarding a proceeding must include all parties to the proceeding, except as otherwise authorized. 37 C.F.R. § 42.5(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions include ministerial communications with support staff (e.g., to arrange a conference call); conference calls or hearings in which opposing counsel declines to participate; informing the Board in one proceeding of the existence or status of a related Board proceeding; and reference to a pending case in support of a general proposition (e.g., citing a published opinion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arranging a Conference Call with the Board
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties should meet and confer before requesting a conference call; if meet-and-confer fails, a party may request a conference call with the Board to raise and resolve procedural issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to explain why the call is needed and what materials (e.g., exhibits) may be used. Notify the Board if a court reporter will be provided; if a reporter is present, the party retaining the reporter must notify the panel at the start and file the transcript as an exhibit within one week of receiving it. The Board envisions most procedural issues will be handled in days via conference call.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to Participate in Conference Calls or Hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has discretion to permit a hearing or conference call to proceed even if a party refuses to participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a party refuses to participate, the Board may require additional safeguards (e.g., recording the communication and entering the recording into the record).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing a Motion to Seal and Proposed Protective Order
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may file a motion to seal that contains a proposed protective order; a protective order is not entered by default and must be approved and entered by the Board. 37 C.F.R. § 42.54.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protective orders may be issued for good cause to protect confidential information. The document will be protected on receipt of the motion and remain so pending the decision. If the motion is denied, the submitting party may seek expungement of the submitted confidential information; otherwise it may be publicly disclosed. Appendix B provides guidelines (including a Default Protective Order).

rubrics_metrics.name: Default Protective Order — Who May Access Confidential Information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Default Protective Order sets categories of persons who may access protective-order material: parties (patent owners and named parties), party representatives of record, retained experts (subject to non-competitor certification), in-house counsel, support personnel reasonably necessary to assist, and USPTO employees/representatives who need access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employees/consultants (other than in-house counsel and their support staff) who will receive confidential information must sign the Acknowledgement and are extended access only upon agreement of the parties or Board order; the opposing party bears the burden of proving why access should be restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default Protective Order — Protection and Handling Obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons receiving confidential information must take reasonable care to maintain confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable efforts include secure storage inaccessible to unauthorized persons, efforts no less rigorous than recipient's usual confidentiality protections, ensuring support personnel understand obligations, limiting copying to a reasonable number of copies and maintaining records of locations of copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default Protective Order — Filing Procedures for Confidential Material
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for filing confidential material with the Board: file under seal with a non-confidential description and reasons for confidentiality, or when only some information is confidential, file both confidential and non-confidential redacted versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The non-confidential version must clearly indicate locations of redactions; redacted information remains under seal pending Board determination. A party may oppose a Motion to Seal and seek a hearing; while motion is pending, the challenged portions are not disclosed to opposed persons but disclosure to non-opposed persons may proceed and the motion does not toll other deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default Protective Order — Confidential Testimony Procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness may preliminarily designate the entirety of testimony and transcriptions as confidential on the record during testimony, pending review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within ten days of receiving the transcript the witness (or representative) must identify which portions to maintain as confidential and provide reasons; designated portions are maintained under seal pending Board determination after possible motion or sua sponte review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default Protective Order — Acknowledgement Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person receiving confidential information must sign an Acknowledgement (under penalty of perjury) before receiving such information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Acknowledgement must state the person has read and agrees to be bound by the Protective Order, will use the information only for the proceeding, limit access to necessary support personnel (who must be informed of the Order), and submit to the Office's jurisdiction for enforcement. Parties must retain signed Acknowledgements and produce them on request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default Protective Order — Disposal of Confidential Information
rubrics_metrics.description: After final termination of the proceeding (including appeals) or after time to appeal expires, parties must destroy confidential information and certify destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, within one month after final termination each party shall assemble all copies of confidential information (including copies provided to representatives and experts), destroy them, and provide a certification of destruction to the producing party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifications and Adoption of Protective Orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may propose modifications to the Default Protective Order; the Board will generally accept agreed changes that are consistent with the integrity and efficient administration of proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will presumptively accept reasonable additional tiers (e.g., 'Attorneys’ Eyes Only') if adequately defined, but will not accept overly inclusive definitions encouraging broad labeling. When proceedings parallel a district court case, parties may propose adopting a district court protective order provided unnecessary or inappropriate provisions (e.g., certain computer-source-code protections or prosecution bars) are removed and conflicting terms with Board procedures are deleted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery Standard by Proceeding Type
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may seek discovery similar to that under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, but the standard for additional discovery varies by proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'interests of justice' standard applies in IPR and derivation proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 42.51(b)(2)); a 'good cause' standard applies in PGR and CBM proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 42.224). PGR and CBM are broader in scope (may include §§ 101 and 112), so good-cause is more liberal; discussion in the guide focuses on 'interests of justice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Garmin Factors for Authorizing Additional Discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining authorization for additional discovery under the 'interests of justice' standard, the Board primarily considers the five Garmin factors from Garmin Int’l, Inc. v. Cuozzo Speed Techs. LLC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five factors: (1) More Than A Possibility And Mere Allegation — requester must show beyond speculation that useful evidence will be uncovered and show the party already possesses evidence/reasoning supporting that; 'useful' means favorable substantive value, not merely relevant/admissible. (2) Litigation Positions And Underlying Basis — discovery of the other party’s litigation positions and the basis is typically not necessary (contention interrogatories usually not permitted). (3) Ability To Generate Equivalent Information By Other Means — information the requester can reasonably assemble without discovery weighs against granting. (4) Easily Understandable Instructions — requests should be clear. (5) Requests Not Overly Burdensome To Answer — must be sensible and reasonably tailored given IPR's expedited nature (financial, personnel, and schedule burdens considered). Parties seeking authorization should be prepared to address these factors during a conference call with the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonly Sought Additional Discovery Topics and Tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Two frequently sought discovery areas are identifying real parties-in-interest (RPI) and secondary evidence of non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrowly focused, appropriately tailored requests on these issues may be permitted (examples of both grants and denials are provided). Overbroad, unfocused, or unduly burdensome requests (e.g., broad copying allegations without showing how feature is embodied in claims) are likely to be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live Testimony — When Permitted and Factors to Consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Live testimony is permitted only in limited circumstances where witness demeanor is critical to assessing credibility; cross-examination may occur in presence of an administrative patent judge at deposition or oral argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted examples include where derivation is at issue, allegations of misconduct, or an inventor’s testimony to antedate references (K-40 Electronics). Live testimony is case-by-case; factors (K-40) include importance of testimony to the case (possibly case-dispositive) and whether the witness is a fact witness (favoring live testimony). Expert credibility often hinges on theory plausibility rather than demeanor. Testimony not previously provided in declaration may be considered new evidence and not permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition Claim Construction Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner who believes a claim term requires express construction must include a statement identifying a proposed construction and where intrinsic and/or extrinsic evidence supports that meaning; a petitioner may instead state that no express construction is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent owner may respond and propose additional terms; the petitioner may reply to new constructions but cannot raise new claim construction issues that were not raised in its petition. If the Board raises a claim construction issue, both parties get an opportunity to respond prior to the final written decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 112(f) (Means-Plus-Function) Construction Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claim language may be construed under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), a petitioner must provide a construction that includes both the claimed function and the specific portions of the specification that describe the structure, material, or acts corresponding to each claimed function. 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party may explain why § 112(f) should or should not apply. Failure to address § 112(f) risks not satisfying 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction Standard — District Court (Phillips) Standard Applies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board applies the same claim construction standard that would be used in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b) (Phillips v. AWH), per final rule changes; this applies to IPR, PGR, and CBM petitions filed on or after Nov. 13, 2018.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will construe claims and proposed substitute claims based on the record of the proceeding — claim language, specification, prosecution history, and relevant extrinsic evidence. Parties should point to specific portions of specification, prosecution history, and extrinsic evidence and explain relevancy. Each party bears the burden of providing sufficient support for constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and Weight of Prior Claim Constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any prior claim construction determination in a civil action or ITC proceeding, if timely made of record in the PTAB proceeding, will be considered and given appropriate weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-exclusive factors for weight include similarity between district/ITC record and the PTAB record, and whether the prior construction is final or interlocutory. Parties should submit prior constructions as soon as available (preferably with petition, preliminary response, or response). After institution, supplemental information rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.123, 42.223) require authorization to submit new material, and if >1 month after institution the movant must show why it could not have been obtained earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Parties' Statements from Other Proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may consider statements regarding claim scope or claim construction made by patent owners or petitioners in other proceedings (including statements submitted under 35 U.S.C. § 301(a)) if timely made of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To ensure consideration, a party should specifically point out such statements and explain how they support or contradict a proposed construction. Each party bears the burden of providing sufficient support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Owner Preliminary Response — Permissible Arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may file a preliminary response (within three months after the Notice of Filing Date Accorded to Petition) presenting arguments and supporting evidence to demonstrate that no review should be instituted. 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.107(a),(b), 42.207(a),(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of arguments include: (1) petitioner is statutorily barred; (2) asserted references are not printed publications; (3) prior art lacks a material limitation; (4) prior art does not teach/suggest the petitioner's combination; (5) petitioner's claim interpretation is unreasonable; (6) for § 101 grounds in PGR/CBM, explanation why claims are patent-eligible; (7) reasons to exercise Director’s discretion to deny institution under 35 U.S.C. § 314 and/or § 325(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimonial Evidence at the Preliminary Stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimonial evidence may be submitted with a preliminary response, but genuine issues of material fact created by such evidence will be viewed in the light most favorable to the petitioner solely for purposes of deciding whether to institute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No negative inference if patent owner does not present testimonial evidence. If trial is instituted, the petitioner generally has opportunity to cross-examine declarants; parties may withdraw declarants submitted at preliminary stage (and withdrawing typically avoids deposition on the withdrawn declaration). A petitioner may seek leave to file a reply to preliminary-response testimonial evidence (must show good cause); such replies are not expected to be commonly granted due to institution time constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Owner Election to Waive Preliminary Response or Statutory Disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may elect to waive the preliminary response (no adverse inference will be drawn) or file a statutory disclaimer of challenged claims to streamline proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all challenged claims are disclaimed, Board will terminate the proceeding. If some claims remain, the institution decision will be based on the remaining claims. Once trial is instituted, the Board may decline to consider preliminary-response arguments not renewed in the patent owner response (waiver).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution of Trial — Statutory Standard and Director’s Discretion (35 U.S.C. §§ 314(a), 324(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board institutes trial on behalf of the Director and must consider whether statutory institution standards are satisfied; the Director has discretion to deny a petition (Cuozzo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Director's discretion is informed by 35 U.S.C. §§ 316(b) and 326(b) to consider effects on economy, integrity of patent system, Office efficiency, and ability to timely complete proceedings. A petitioner is entitled to a final written decision addressing all claims it challenged once trial is instituted (SAS Institute).

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic Factors for Follow-On Petitions and Discretion in Institution
rubrics_metrics.description: In exercising discretion to institute (especially for 'follow-on' petitions challenging the same patent), the Board considers the non-exclusive General Plastic factors to assess impacts on efficiency and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General Plastic factors include: (1) whether same petitioner previously filed a petition directed to the same claims; (2) whether petitioner knew or should have known of the prior art asserted in the second petition when filing the first; (3) whether petitioner had received the patent owner’s preliminary response or Board decision on institution in the first petition when filing the second; (4) length of time between learning of the prior art and filing the second petition; (5) adequacy of petitioner’s explanation for elapsed time between filings; (6) finite resources of the Board; (7) requirement to issue a final determination within one year after institution (35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(11)). The factors are not dispositive or exclusive; they form a balanced assessment along with merits. The Board also considers relationships between different petitioners when different entities file follow-on petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Parallel Proceedings and Prior Presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board will consider whether the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments were previously presented to the Office, district courts, or ITC when exercising discretion to institute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events in other proceedings related to the same patent may justify denying a petition even if threshold standards for institution are met. Parties should account for prior presentations in their filings and the Board may weigh such prior presentations under § 325(d) and related precedent.
